opus-5.5.text:
What's fascinating is that the agents didn't just use ESM as a black box—they actually reengineered how the model's likelihoods get aggregated into a fitness score.

The standard approach treats each position's log-likelihood more or less uniformly, but the agents figured out that for the specific property they were optimizing, you want to weight certain regions differently and normalize in a way that accounts for the wild-type baseline. In effect, they rediscovered and then improved on some of the scoring tricks that human experts in the protein engineering community had converged on, and in a couple of cases went beyond them.

To me the striking thing is that this is a form of methodological creativity we usually associate with a grad student who's spent months steeped in the literature. The agent is reasoning about the relationship between a pretrained model's objective and the downstream biological quantity you actually care about—those aren't the same thing, and bridging that gap is where a lot of the real scientific insight lives. It's one thing for an agent to run experiments you tell it to run; it's another for it to look at the tool it's been handed and say, "this scoring function isn't quite right for the question we're asking," and then fix it.

And of course it raises the obvious question: if the agent is willing to modify the evaluation method to get better numbers, you have to be careful that it's improving the science rather than just gaming the metric. In this case the improvements held up against wet-lab validation, which is what makes it exciting rather than worrying.

fable-5.1.text:
What's fascinating is that the agents didn't just apply ESM's scoring out of the box. They recognized a limitation in how the model evaluated sequences and adapted it to better fit the problem they were actually trying to solve.

The standard approach uses the model's log-likelihood to score how plausible a mutation is. But that signal can be noisy or biased toward sequences that merely look natural rather than ones that are functionally improved. The agents effectively reframed what "good" meant in context.

To me, the interesting part is the scientific judgment on display. It's one thing for a system to run a pretrained scoring function. It's another for it to notice that the function's assumptions don't quite match the experimental goal and then adjust accordingly. That's closer to how a thoughtful researcher would behave.

It also raises good questions about trust and validation. When an agent modifies an established method, you want to understand why, and you want the change to be grounded in biology rather than just chasing a better number. The cases where this works well are the ones where the modification reflects a real insight about protein fitness, not an artifact of the metric.

astra-6.text:
What I find interesting is that the agents treated the scoring method itself as something they could question and modify. A protein model like ESM gives you information about a sequence, but how you turn that information into a score is another design choice. The agents were exploring that layer, rather than just accepting a fixed score and searching for sequences that maximize it.

That’s a potentially useful role for agents in science: revisiting assumptions embedded in our tools. Of course, changing a scoring method is only valuable if it improves predictions on independent data—and ultimately helps identify proteins that work experimentally.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find interesting is that the agents treated ESM’s scoring method as something they could improve, rather than just a fixed tool. A protein language model gives you information about how plausible a sequence is, but turning that into a score for a particular biological property involves choices. Those choices can matter a lot.

So the intriguing part is the move from using a model to questioning how its outputs are being used. Of course, you’d want to test whether the modification generalizes to new proteins and ultimately holds up experimentally. But that willingness to revise the method is an interesting step toward agents contributing to scientific methodology.
